done_when: A thread follow-up starts a turn only when the new batch has a message from an allowed sender, proven by a test where only the root sender is allowed and another person's follow-up gets no reply

findings.body: An unauthorized follow-up can still receive a reply after the root's answer while its runner remains alive. apps/core/src/config/index.ts:503 keeps runners alive for 30 minutes after their last result. During that window, apps/core/src/app/bootstrap/live-execution.ts:268 routes follow-ups directly to the active owner, bypassing this gate. apps/core/src/runtime/live-turn-routing.ts:50 checks only requiredContinuationUserId, which ordinary runs leave unset (group-agent-runner.ts:583); group-queue-live-turn-hooks.ts:31 then forwards the message and starts another visible turn. The new test misses this production path because its runAgent stub immediately returns after emitting the root reply (test/e2e/claim-protocol-two-process.postgres.e2e.test.ts:713–717). Enforce sender authorization on this route and prove that Bob gets no reply when Alice's runner is still waiting after its answer.

findings.body: The required end-to-end proof is excluded from the close command. forge.toml:6 runs npm test, but package.json:86 selects only unit and integration suites, whose configurations exclude apps/core/test/e2e. This test runs only through test:e2e:postgres, invoked by the nightly workflow (.github/workflows/nightly-e2e.yml:93); the PR checks likewise omit it (.github/workflows/ci.yml:157–160). Consequently, the supplied successful close run never exercised this test, and the branch's required checks can pass if it fails. Wire this regression into the required suite with PostgreSQL available.

why: Anyone can get a reply in a thread an allowed person started, because the thread check never looks at who sent the new message
